# Education in Poland
Education in Poland is compulsory and begins with primary school (szkoła podstawowa), where children typically start at age seven (or six with special provisions). Primary education lasts eight years, followed by several forms of upper secondary schooling: general secondary schools (liceum, four years), technical schools (technikum, five years), and basic vocational schools (three years). Upon completing liceum or technikum, students may take the "Matura" exam, granting access to higher education. Vocational pathways are available, and students with disabilities have access to specialized schools. Prior to reforms in 2017, Poland operated a 6+3+3 system, with a separate junior high school (gimnazjum); this was replaced by the current 8+4/5 structure.
Tertiary education in Poland follows the Bologna process, typically offering a three-year bachelor’s degree and a two-year master’s degree, with long-cycle programs for some fields such as medicine. Doctoral programs generally last about three years. The university grading system is numeric, ranging from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest), with increments of 0.5. Foreign language education is common, with English, German, French, Spanish, and Russian frequently offered. Historically, Poland has a strong tradition in education, with roots dating back to the medieval era and early adoption of compulsory schooling. Major reforms in 1999 and 2017 have shaped the current system, improving outcomes as reflected by OECD rankings.
